speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct one question to two ministers, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare. In view of recent statements by scientists concerning radioactivity and its effect on human beings, could these ministers tell the house whether any further consideration is being given

I put this to the minister to my right -to the Canadian government opposing further nuclear explosions and-I put this to the minister to my left-will a further statement be made as to the effect of such things as X-rays, and so on, on human beings?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CANADIAN ATTITUDE TOWARD POSSIBLE POSTPONEMENT OF FURTHER NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) suggests that I might
deal with both questions. With regard to the question addressed to him, as he has indicated previously, in the proposals which were recently discussed in the subcommittee of the disarmament commission in London and in the discussions which took place in that committee last fall at the United Nations, it was clearly demonstrated that the United States, Great Britain, France and Canada gave support to a plan which would provide for the banning of tests within the limits of a comprehensive scheme of disarmament which would work without prejudice to the security of the nations concerned under an adequate system of inspection and control.
With regard to the health aspects of the problem, the situation is that there is now in existence a special scientific committee, created by the United Nations, of 12 states, of which Canada is a member, represented formerly by the late Dr. Cipriani, and now by Dr. Watkinson of the department which I administer.
In addition to that, the Department of National Health and Welfare makes assessments, along with other departments of the government and with the United Nations agencies, to determine the extent of the levels of radioactivity normally produced or produced through recent atomic detonation tests. There is no reason for believing that the health of the people of this country or of other countries has been affected in a way that would cause serious concern. This matter, however, continues to receive careful study and assessment.

speechtext:
Before we begin today's discussions with reference to the estimates of the taxation division, I think it might be well if we were to clear up some of the points that were raised before we adjourned last evening.
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
A question arose with reference to law costs, raised by the hon. member for Perth. In the two votes which you have to consider we are asking for a total of $335,000 for law costs, which represents an increase of $115,000 over what we asked for last year. However, $85,000, or 75 per cent of the increase, was requested to cover the probable maximum fee and costs we would have to pay in connection with the Anaconda appeal which was at that time pending before the privy council. The Anaconda case is one of the most famous cases that we have had to deal with and the final appeal in the matter went before the privy council. I might say that the decision rendered by the privy council was in favour of the Department of National Revenue with reference to the stand it had taken relative to the taxation of this company. If the decision in that case had been rendered against the Department of National Revenue the costs might possibly have been $100,000.
The remaining 25 per cent of the increase is requested in the light of actual expenditures at the time that our estimates were prepared. Careful consideration of the expected number of legal actions indicated that we should provide for an increase of about 10 per cent over the actual expenditures for the previous fiscal year. It is worth noting that last year in the district offices we spent more on law costs than was provided in our estimates. While I am dealing with that particular case, I might say that the total costs in the Anaconda case were $34,976, approximately $35,000. We have provided in the estimates for $85,000 so that we have provided for $50,000 more than we have been actually called upon to spend. It is my intention when we come to the conclusion of the discussion of the item to have one of my colleagues move that this resolution be amended so that item 289 may be reduced by the amount of $50,000.
With reference to legal agents, another point brought up by the hon. member, as hon. members know, litigation on behalf of the government is the responsibility of the Department of Justice, but actually when the Department of National Revenue requires an outside lawyer to take action or to defend it in some proceeding taken against the department it would request assistance from the Department of Justice. In this way the Department of Justice would choose the lawyer to act as its legal agent. The expenses incurred by the Department of Justice are charged against the department for which the work is done. That is the general procedure, so that we have to provide for those costs.
Another item was changes in the act. The hon. member for Perth has repeated certain

items which were mentioned in the hearings before the special committee where the operation of the law seemed to work hardship on certain taxpayers or where there was uncertainty as to its application. My officials are more or less in continual discussion with the officials of the Department of Finance on matters of this kind, and they are all carefully reviewed when the budget is being prepared. I have taken note of the items raised before the special committee and they will be brought to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, prior to the next budget.
With reference to the matter of net worth assessment, the member for Perth has again brought up the question of assessing income tax on a net worth basis. I have spoken on this matter from time to time over the years and I made a rather complete statement on it which is to be found in Hansard of June 23, 1954, pages 6597 to 6600. In his testimony before the special committee the deputy minister indicated that the department does not favour this method of assessment where an assessment based on actual facts is possible. However, the department does have a responsibility to see that all taxpayers discharge their proper liability and in the absence of books and records assessment on the net worth basis is often the only way open to the assessor. The assessor is instructed to use this basis only when all other methods of determining the correct income and tax liability fail and to explain the method to the taxpayers when it is used.
Another matter which was brought up had to do with capital gains. The hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre suggested that the department was improperly trying to tax certain profits commonly known as capital gains. First of all, I should like to reiterate that the taxation division has purely administrative responsibilities. It does not make law. It only applies the Income Tax Act and the Dominion Succession Duty Act according to the terms in which those two statutes have been passed by parliament. Naturally, in interpreting the wording of these statutes the law officers of the division must try to find the meaning that the courts would give to them. As cases go to the courts and decisions are rendered, they are given indications which assist them in their interpretation.
The distinction between capital gains and business profits has not changed over the years. The difference was well explained by Lord Justice Clark in the case of California Copper Syndicate v. Harris in the British courts in 1904.
Supply-National Revenue

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON TELEVISION PROGRAM
speechtext: Which Harris?

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON TELEVISION PROGRAM
speechtext:
He said this, and I quote:
It is quite a well settled principle in dealing with questions ... of income tax that where the owner of an ordinary investment chooses to realize it and obtains a greater price for it than he originally acquired it at, the enhanced price is not a profit . . . assessable for income tax. But it is equally well established that enhanced values obtained from realization or conversion of securities may be so assessable where what is done is not merely a realization or change of investment but an act done in what is truly the carrying on, or carrying out, of a business. The simplest case is that of a person or association of persons buying and selling land or securities speculatively, in order to make gain, dealing with such investment as a business and thereby seeking to make profits . . .
What is the line which separates the two classes of cases may be difficult to define and each case must be considered according to the facts; the question to be determined being-"is the sum of the gain that has been made a mere enhancement of value or realizing a security, or is it a gain made in the operation of business in carrying out a scheme of profit making?"
That is the end of the quotation. This quotation has been cited repeatedly in subsequent cases both by the English and by the Canadian courts. It has been repeatedly said that each case must be determined on its own merits. The courts take into consideration various factors which include the intention of the taxpayer, the number or frequency of the transactions, the relation of the transactions to the taxpayer's regular business, the nature of the transaction and the course of conduct of the taxpayer. None of these factors are deciding in themselves but all the circumstances must be regarded as a whole.
I do not think that the courts have had greater difficulty in deciding these matters than they have with other legal problems which are continually coming before them. Perhaps there has been more interest in the matter in recent years because the income tax appeal board has provided an easy method of settling differences between the taxpayer and the department and the period of high prosperity through which we have been passing has given many people an opportunity to make side profits in property dealings.
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Tax Journal of November-December 1955 has a very interesting article called "The Capital Gains Scare". It is written by Robert Tresilian who I presume is an anonymous writer. I am not going over the whole of the article, although it is very interesting reading for anyone who is interested in this particular subject. However, I should like to quote this much:
Some weeks ago the press reported that a case was to be heard shortly by the tax appeal board in which an appeal was to be made from an

Supply-National Revenue assessment on gains made in the stock exchange. Though no such case has yet been reported, the press announcement appears to have caused a minor panic.
I think most hon. members are familiar with the law of the United States where there is a tax of 25 per cent on capital gains throughout the year. I am not going to go through the whole of the article, but I am going to read the conclusion which is very significant to me at least.
To conclude, it would appear that the concern expressed by the press is unfounded. The few court decisions to which references have been made are merely evidence of the process of separating the wolves from the flock, the former- being those enterprising persons who attempt to wear the sheepskin of the ordinary investor, while carrying on the ordinary trading, businesses or ventures which the law has always declared to be taxable.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, there is the question asked by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) with reference to the deductibility of donations for political purposes. I have announced the policy of the department, and that has been the policy of the department during the past 11 years I have been there. He referred to the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and the reason I gave the answer I did that day was that I did not hear the whole of the question. But that is the general principle which has been followed, and I have discussed it with every deputy minister I have had. It is the policy which has been carried out. After a firm has paid its taxes, if it wishes to make a donation for political purposes it is not my concern what they do with the money or to whom they give it.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in answer to that, there is no definition in the law of what constitutes a capital gain. On several occasions it has been brought up when we have had the preliminary meetings on the budget with the finance committee, and the best legal advice is that up to date they have not been able to define what constitutes a capital gain.

In the discussion of this first item of general administration of income tax yesterday the hon. member for Dauphin, in his opening remarks, referred to the net worth statement as it affects farmers in the province of Manitoba and expressed his grievances with the attitude taken at times by the officials of the Department of National Revenue in dealing with farmers and in continuing at times to make a net worth statement which is not in accordance with the net return, I would say, of the farms in the previous three or five years. His remarks in respect to the net worth statement were very brief. I listened attentively to what he had to say, and in his first remarks and in the latter part of his speech which I read carefully this morning I notice that of the five columns of his speech four columns refer to the question which was asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on April

9, which I shall read. It was addressed to the Minister of National Revenue and is recorded at page 2729 of Hansard, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Revenue? Will the minister re-examine the income tax files of the breweries of Manitoba to ascertain whether any of them claimed income tax deductibility for the contributions they made, as revealed in Winnipeg last week, to the Liberal, Conservative and Social Credit parties of Manitoba?
Then, of course, the hon. member for Dauphin continued his remarks on this question and he referred to the report which was discussed at Winnipeg at that time, which was issued by the royal commission established by the provincial government of Manitoba with respect to the liquor situation in that province. I shall quote the remarks made by the hon. member for Dauphin, as reported at page 5010 of Hansard:
In that statement you will find that the representative of the breweries stated that not only did the breweries of Manitoba make cash contributions to the political parties within the province of Manitoba but they made them also to the federal political parties.
I may say here that by using the plural "political parties" he does not include the C.C.F. party. I continue:
That immediately, of course, involves the consideration of this parliament.
In the last paragraph on the same page we find the following:
In case the minister or the committee is in doubt about what happened in Manitoba, may I refer them to some of the newspaper headlines. For example, the Winnipeg Free Press of April 4, 1956, carried this headline, "Breweries Bare Gifts to Three Parties; All But C.C.F. Shared $28,075 since 1945".
The remarks continue with respect to these gifts made only to the major political parties of the province of Manitoba. The members of the C.C.F. party stand up in this parliament and in the province of Manitoba with halos over their heads and rejoice that they receive no contributions from any corporation, either in Manitoba or throughout Canada. That is not a clear picture of the situation. We all know that political organizations have certain work to do and they have expenses to meet, and it is well known that contributions are received to help defray those expenses.
Our friends of the C.C.F. party are trying to set up a different picture. They say they receive no cash for their political organizations throughout western Canada. As I say, they go around with halos over their heads telling us that they receive no contributions from any corporation. But that is not the clear picture at all. The reason I rise today is to set out the situation that exists in Manitoba,
Supply-National Revenue especially in my own city of St. Boniface. I want to indicate the way in which the C.C.F. raise their political funds. They are now operating one of the largest gambling joints in the province of Manitoba right in my own city of St. Boniface.
A few years ago the C.C.F. party applied to the provincial secretary of Manitoba for a charter to operate what was called the commonwealth recreation society. This was being formed in order to round up all their friends. I call them their friends because the attitude they have taken in the past on public platforms in Manitoba is that they are the only friends of those Canadian citizens who are receiving social benefits, of the farmers and of labour.
We all know that members of the C.C.F. must contribute a certain percentage of their indemnity to the party funds, and no doubt in addition they receive contributions from individuals. But once this charter was obtained the picture was different. I should like to place on the record the names of the directors of that organization. I think I am fair in doing this because these names are taken from a public document.
One director is W. C. Leitkie, who is well known to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He has been an organizer for the C.C.F. and is an employee of Canadian National Telegraphs. Another is A. R. Paulley, member of the legislative assembly for Kildonan-Transcona. Another is Dave Mulligan, alderman for ward 1 in the city of Winnipeg. The last is none other than the Rev. Lloyd Stinson, the provincial leader of the C.C.F. party.
This recreation society was formed for the purpose of holding social evenings with their friends, but they operate bingo games. These were first started in the city of Winnipeg but the law officers advised the members of the C.C.F. that bingo or any form of gambling would not be allowed in Winnipeg. So they crossed over the Red river to St. Boniface and rented large quarters from an individual where they could operate this commonwealth recreation society. I might say that last year the individual from whom they rented these quarters was fined $16,000 for having made fraudulent income tax returns.
If the C.C.F. intended to operate this for fraternal purposes or as a social gathering they would probably have a bingo game once a week or twice a month. We all know that organizations in certain parts of Canada, particularly in Ottawa, service clubs and the like, operate bingo games possibly once a month. Valuable prizes are given, sometimes

As I say, these people go around the prairies with halos over their heads saying that they receive no contributions from corporations, yet they tax their friends so much a night when they attend thirteen times a month at this recreation society. The total received would be far more than the $30,000 received from 1945 to 1955 from the breweries in that province.
I bring this matter to the attention of the committee because of the remarks yesterday by the hon. member for Dauphin. Mr. Chairman, the minister has reiterated the general tenor of his remarks in the committee when he said that his department was concerned only with the administration of the act and disclaimed any responsibility for the actual enactment of income tax legislation.
However, it seems to me that the minister must recognize that he, in his capacity as a


member of the executive, has probably more influence than any other member except the Minister of Finance himself with regard to the formulation of policy. I think this is borne out by some of the remarks of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. On the evening when he presented the budget to the house, the Minister of Finance referred to the fact that he and the Minister of National Revenue conferred. I think he used the expression, "the Minister of National Revenue and I have given considerable thought" to certain aspects of the legislation. I do not doubt that that is true. It would be very odd indeed if they were not in conference almost continuously as to the administration of the department and also the policies that the government proposed to put into effect.
I have just been looking back on the budget debate. I cannot find the actual place but I remember that on that evening the Minister of Finance tendered his thanks to the Minister of National Revenue for the collecting of substantial sums, but I must say that I did not hear him proffer the same thanks to the taxpayers who paid those sums. No doubt it was an oversight, and possibly the Minister of Finance would permit me to make that correction in his remarks at this time. Because I believe that the Minister of National Revenue must have some influence on the forming of policy, I believe that there are some things that should be said in this debate on the estimates of his department. A few of the things that I wish to bring up now, I did comment on in committee, but I should like to have them on the record of this house. Now that the Minister of Finance is in the house also, I hope that he will likewise bear in mind the suggestions I make.
In the first place I should like to refer to the practice of the department of taxing rental revenue as investment income when it comes to the taxpayer from an estate or trust. I draw attention to the remarks I made in the committee, which were to the effect that it has been ruled in court on many occasions that income does not change its character by reason of passing through a trustee to a beneficiary. As a matter of fact, I think the rule is so well established that it scarcely needs to be mentioned, but I believe that that should be borne in mind when we consider the practice of the department of assessing income from trusts or estates as investment income without regard for the source of that income.
On the T3 form, the estate or trust return, in the section that deals with surtax on

investment income, there is a little note to which I drew attention previously in the committee. It says:
Rental income from real property and income from a business or farm operated by the executor or trustee are not subject to surtax in his hands.
Yet on the new T1 general form, the only place where you can report income from estates or trust is in the investment income space. That in turn is carried forward to be reported for the purposes of surtax on page 2. It seems to me that this is a matter which the government should consider.
Since the Minister of National Revenue disclaims responsibility for policy, then I appeal to other members of the government to consider this in the executive and, because there is apparently no foundation in law for this departmental practice, to see that steps are taken to have rental income assessed for tax purposes as it should be, without regard to whether or not it passes through intermediate hands before reaching the ultimate beneficiary. I suggest that that could be done simply by making space available on the T 1 general form for the reporting of income from rental accruing to a beneficiary from an estate or trust. It would be a very simple matter to arrange, and I suggest that consideration be given to it.
There was another question which I brought up in the committee and about which I wish to speak for a few minutes this afternoon. That is the apparent discrepancy in the allowance of charitable donations. In speaking on this particular aspect in the committee I drew attention to the fact that apparently in some sections of the country there had grown up a practice of allowing donations to the sum of $25 unsubstantiated by receipts. I admit that the minister and the officials of his department expressed surprise that this was the case but since the day when we discussed that in the committee, because of the surprise which was shown by the government minister and his officials, I checked into it again and I find that that practice has been adopted in certain centres. I fancy that bringing the matter to light in this way will result in a directive from the department to the effect that taxpayers in all parts of the country must be treated in precisely the same manner. If it is the department's desire to allow donations up to $25 without receipts, then that allowance should be made to all taxpayers. Whether or not a portion of their taxable donations is substantiated by receipts, they should be allowed to add to that amount $25 for sundry causes. I suggest to the minister that they should do one or the other; either they should allow it to everyone or they should allow it to no one. I do not
Supply-National Revenue believe there should be any discrimination with regard to these allowances.
There is another matter which was discussed in the committee and about which I should like to speak this afternoon. That is the interpretation that has been placed on clause 11 (1) (j), which resulted in the disallowance of alimony in a specific case which I cited in the committee. I do not intend to go into the details of this case. I merely wish to quote Mr. Fordham, a copy of whose judgment in this particular case I hold in my hand. In giving his judgment he set out clause 11 (1) (j) and he made these remarks:
Much to the taxpayer's surprise, however, the minister disallowed such deductions and ruled that they did not come within the purview of the provision set out above. At the hearing it became clear that this was because the word "alimony" did not appear after "divorce" in the fourth line of paragraph (j), above. An appeal to the board duly followed.
Then Mr. Fordham went on to say:
The matter reveals for the first time, where the board is concerned, what appears to be a remarkable and unfortunate oversight or omission in the drafting of the foregoing enactment. Although alimony, as such, is clearly deductible by the payer when a court has made an award of alimony in a decree, order or judgment for divorce, or a husband or wife have executed a separation agreement providing for the payment of alimony, subsection (1)	(j) does not take cognizance of an
action for alimony alone. No reference to such a proceeding is to be found in its wording. Hence, the unfortunate appellant cannot have the relief that is ordinarily afforded to those obligated to pay alimony periodically. The words "judicial separation" do not assist him, as the Ontario courts are without jurisdiction to entertain actions for judicial separation.
Those are the words of Mr. Fordham. You can no doubt look them up. However, the point which he makes is a point which I ask the government to consider, namely, whether or not clause 11 (1) (j) should be amended by insertion of the word "alimony" in that clause to permit the deduction of alimony where it is a matter of agreement and has been sanctioned by the courts without going through the formalities of divorce proceedings. I trust the government will consider that because it seems to me a grave injustice that people who accept their financial responsibilities in this manner should have such allowances removed from their list of recognized deductions for income tax purposes.
Over the past few years, Mr. Chairman, there have been a number of pleas made in the house for the removal of the floor on medical expenses, and I could not speak on the estimates of national revenue without mentioning this particular point and once more urging the government, as I am sure other members also will, to remove that floor. The arguments in favour of so doing have
5022	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Revenue been set out on numerous occasions. I do not intend to go into them at any length this afternoon. I would be merely reiterating arguments which I have made previously and which other members of the house have made. I still believe it would be a sound move and I think also it would be just simple justice to people who, in time of great need, are forced to pay out large sums which undoubtedly causes them considerable distress, and it seems to me they should be permitted to take all of these items as deductions and not just the portion in excess of a certain percentage of their income.
There is one other matter I should like to bring before the house this afternoon. I refer to the position in which the selfemployed person, whether in business or the professions, finds himself with regard to the building up of retirement funds. There have been a great many articles written on this matter as well as letters to the newspapers and presentations made to members of parliament and to the government. I have in my hand a letter written by a well known Hamilton doctor to the Hamilton Spectator in which he describes the situation in which a physician finds himself with regard to setting up some sort of scheme to give him security late in his life. He says in part that the physician in attempting to set up an estate invests in annuities or some other insurance scheme to ensure security later in life but because he is self-employed this deduction cannot be allowed. He draws attention in a personal letter to me to the presentation to members of parliament by the Canadian Medical Association which requested in part tax deferment on personal contributions to annuities or other retirement funds.
I want to emphasize once more that in speaking in this vein this afternoon I am not speaking solely on behalf of professional people because I think there are a great many businessmen, small businessmen particularly, who find themselves in precisely the same position as those who operate professional practices. In the letter from the Canadian Medical Association accompanying the presentation to members of parliament they draw attention to an article by Dr. T. James Quintin of Sherbrooke which appeared in the October 1, 1955, issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal. In Dr. Quintin's article he made some very pertinent comments. He started out by quoting part of a statement taken from the Millar Tucker report to the British House of Commons on the taxation treatment of provisions for retirement, and I should like to read into the record two sentences that he quoted.


It has to be remembered that the law of income tax is not one of the laws of nature. It is purely man made and the principles governing the imposition of the tax therefore depend on the will of the creator.
Dr. Quintin refers to this statement taken from the Millar Tucker report and he comments that it is used in referring to the changes needed in the income tax law as it applies to self-employed persons. Dr. Quintin refers only to physicians, but as I said before I refer to all self-employed persons. Dr. Quintin goes on to say:
It is they, the self-savers, who suffer from this discrimination in our present Canadian Income Tax Act, as opposed to the pension savers who, because they work for a group or an industry, are allowed postponement of income tax on a portion of their income, if they are eligible for membership in approved pension plans.
I do not intend to read much more of what Dr. Quintin has to say but his remarks seemed to me to be so pertinent that I could not improve on them myself. Therefore, if the house will permit me, I should like to read one or two paragraphs. Dr. Quintin says:
The physician suffers with all the self-employed under the inequities of the present system, but he suffers more because he requires the longest training amongst the professional groups.
Some members might challenge that but nevertheless this is his presentation. He says:
His earnings are concentrated in a shorter period of time, and during these peak years he is often taxed in a higher income bracket than if he had had his income spread out over a longer tax period.
Then he goes on to point out the effect which this situation is having on the profession in general and he makes this comment:
Instances of the "old doctor" who has had to hang on to his practice because he has nothing on which to retire are too well known to all of us. Or the middle-aged physician who is ill and who has served his hospital, his patients and his community well, and yet can't take it easy or retire, as he was not able even at his peak years to save after paying his income tax.
Then speaking of the young doctor he says.
Where are the young graduates who could be our much-sought-after general practitioners or self-employed family doctors? They are to be found in the clinic groups or among the company doctors, where among other things they will have a certain security which appeals, and a guaranteed retirement income paid for by income tax relief allowed to them because they are not selfemployed.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, this situation, apart from being unfair, does little to encourage individual initiative.
I should like to refer to another source, namely a brief, if such it can be called or rather a memorandum as they describe it, sent by the Canadian Dental Association to the government with respect to the deductibility of pension payments from taxable

income. In the first paragraph of this memorandum which is headed "Fundamental basis of Proposals", the dental association has this to say.
In making this presentation, we feel justified in claiming that we are not asking the government to consider any new principle for surely it is long accepted and incorporated in income tax legislation that is just, and desirable as a matter of public policy, that the individual who has laboured throughout the productive years of his life should be rewarded over a longer period than his actual service: that some of the income of the productive years should be deferred to the years when work is no longer possible.
I am sure the minister would agree with me, Mr. Chairman, and the Minister of Finance also, that this was, after all, the way in which people in this country have planned their lives for many years. The income tax is a comparatively new field. Years and years ago persons were able to save from income and lay aside their savings. Then when their years of activity had ceased they were able to have funds with which to support themselves for the rest of their lives. But in periods of high taxation it is almost impossible to save sufficient to guarantee a retirement income purely from personal savings. So there has grown up over the years the demand for an insured period of retirement and schemes have been promoted and have become popular in industry. Even the government itself has such a scheme which is available to purchasers. But I should draw attention here to the fact that a man who subscribes to a retirement scheme and who is employed in industry, where that scheme is recognized by the government, is permitted to deduct the premiums from income for taxation assessment. However, a selfemployed person can purchase precisely the same kind of annuity from the same source, pay the same premiums and be allowed no deductions. It just does not seem to add up to equitable treatment, and I trust that the government will give some consideration to this extremely important mattei.
In closing these remarks I should like to read again two short paragraphs from the brief of the dental association:
We believe the government desires, as a matter of good public policy, the maintenance of income as a stabilizing factor in the economy of the nation, contributing to the maintenance of employment and the general well-being.
Finally, we believe it contrary to good public policy that professional men, however able in their prime, should be compelled as a matter of personal subsistence, to continue practice after their faculties are impaired.

Usually the work of the assessors and inspectors of the income tax division is not an easy one. Their task is not pleasant when they have to investigate mistakes, sometimes deliberate mistakes, made in a financial statement. But in


democracy there are, between civilized people, certain limits beyond which it is nothing less than abuse, which borders on sadism. Witness the following instance of a case recently reported in one of the cities of this province.
One fine spring morning, six or seven automobiles drove into town, each carrying a member of the R.C.M.P. and one or two accountants from the income tax division. At exactly the same time, a group calls simultaneously at the office and at the home of three professional people of the city; the man in charge shows to the wife or the secretary an authorization from the Deputy Minister of Finance and a search warrant signed by the president of the Exchequer Court. The two documents, requested by a French Canadian and concerning French Canadians, and authorizing a complete search of the home of a French Canadian, are drafted exclusively in English. But that is of no importance to those gentlemen who give a brief explanation of their significance, without bothering to make sure that the meaning of the document is fully understood, (French legal texts are already not too easy to understand, let alone the meaning of such a document for one who is not conversant with legal terms or with English) and they immediately ask to be led to the bedroom or the office of the boss. The moment chosen is of course one when the head of the family is away from his home and from his office. Then begins a complete search; those people even take upon themselves to read excerpts from the personal diary or the intimate correspondence of the husband or wife. Nothing can be done to avoid that search of one's treasures. If permission is refused, everything will be taken away and then . . . When the victim of such a brutal investigation arrives, having been advised by telephone, and tries to discuss the matter with them, the investigators, relying on their power and their position, reply politely, but without giving any definite answer, except the following: "We have been instructed to take with us anything that may pertain to accounting. We are entitled to see everything, to look everywhere and to examine all documents, whether personal or not." And search of the premises goes on; nothing is overlooked, not even the box of sanitary napkins or the garbage pails. The investigators take away all documents they see fit to seize, without giving any receipt for the items taken away, leaving it up to the owner to list them and make a claim (what chance would he have to be heard?) if everything which has been taken is not given back. Except for the use of a revolver and brutal treatment of women and children, one would think that we were living behind the Iron Curtain! It remains that such a method of investigation is unjustified, if steps have not been taken previously to obtain the required information and such attacks are led first against respectable citizens. Secret police methods and intimidation have no place in a true democracy; one is led to wonder whether all that deliberate and systematic campaign by the government against certain professions, does not aim to lower their prestige and give it a freer hand in taking certain political steps. But there is one thing that is even more serious, and it is the use in such cases of documents in English only. When the authorities force the door of a taxpayer, violate the privacy of his home, and take contemptible and despicable means to find fault with him and take away his money, that is already more or less democratic, but when insult is added to injury by the fact that no respect is shown for the victim's mother tongue, that goes beyond the limits and adds insult to brutality. That also shows the spirit which prevails in the income tax division, a contempt for the taxpayer, especially the French-speaking tax-

payer. Let us hope that one of our members of parliament will rise in the house and mention the fact.
I think this letter speaks for itself, Mr. Chairman, and does not call for any comments. However, I have another duty i.e., to tell the government, and more especially the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), to give strict orders to stop such abuse at once.

I have spoken about this on a number of occasions in the past and I believe the minister has already made quite a lengthy statement and has given the pages of Hansard on which I could find it. But the point is that I have received a number of protests from farmers, and the protests they have made are not covered by the statement made by the minister. I should like at this time to draw these to the attention of the minister.
I am not complaining regarding the type of inspectors sent out to get these forms filled. As a matter of fact, the men that have been sent out to the part of the country I come from have been men with very great experience in agriculture. Farmers have said to me that they know all the answers and that you could not get away with anything. I am not saying that the government should not send out men like that. I think it is good that they know the full score. But I would point out that this is a situation where the odds are loaded heavily in favour of the Department of National Revenue. The inspector knows all about agriculture and he knows all about income tax; the farmer knows about agriculture but he does not know much about the income tax. Therefore it is possible for the inspector to put many things over on the farmer-I would not say intentionally- perhaps unintentionally. I think that often happens. It seems to me that too often the inspector is too much interested in trying to collect more revenue than in just collecting the amount of revenue that the government is entitled to obtain under the Income Tax Act.
I am going to give the minister a few illustrations of what I mean. First of all, it seems to me that, as soon as the farmer goes into the office, the inspector should immediately explain to him the purpose of the visit. The minister says that they do that, but unfortunately they apparently often enter into what might be called a friendly conversation. I have never been in myself and I have to depend on what farmers have told me but, in view of the fact that quite a number of farmers have told me a very similar story, I think there must be something in it. For instance, they say that when they walk in they are treated very courteously by the inspector. The inspector says, "I'll bet you have a difficult job with the prices you are called upon to pay now". The farmer agrees with him. Then he says, "I suppose you find
Supply-National Revenue the cost of living high these days". The farmer agrees. Then the farmer agrees that the cost of living has gone up to perhaps $2,000 a year or some other figure. Right then and there the farmer has two strikes against him. Then they get down to business, but the farmer has already put his foot in it. Then the inspector explains the purpose of the visit. By then possibly the farmer begins to realize that he has committed certain indiscretions.
It seems to me that the very first thing that should be explained to the farmer is that according to his income tax returns the increase in his capital seemed to be greater than his return of income would warrant. That should be explained at the very start. That is done, but unfortunately not at the very start. Very often the farmer is able to give a satisfactory explanation. He is able to explain that his father has given him some capital or made a loan to buy machinery, which accounts for the increase in capital that did not appear to be justified in the report of income; or it may be the result of a small legacy.
The inspector should be very careful to see that no item is included in the cost of living that is deductible or, if it is deductible, he should be very careful to see that it is actually deducted. I could give an example. This is a case that I brought up with the department in Ottawa and it was straightened out, but there must be many similar cases that have not been brought up, with the result that the farmer has been charged tax that he should not have been charged. In this case, a farmer having the cost of living expenditures made up, admitted that he had made a charitable donation of $240, and that was included in his cost of living. That should have been also allowed as a deduction. The farmer had never received a deduction for it, but it was shown as cost of living. The inspector should also have been very careful at that moment to see that that $240 was included as a deduction. Consequently, of course, the farmer had to pay an additional tax as a result of having that charitable donation shown as a cost of living expenditure, and without being given any credit for a deduction.
There is another point, and this is, I think, a little harder to deal with. From what I have gathered from farmers, if they bring this matter to the attention of the inspector it is allowed, but if they do not bring it up it is not allowed. In a case of this kind, where the inspector has all the experience and knowledge of the act, he has a responsibility to draw to the attention of the farmers where they can cut down their taxes by

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take only a few minutes in order to refer to the statement made by the hon. member for St. Boniface earlier this afternoon in reference to what I had to say yesterday. I regret, and I am sure he will also regret it on reflection, that the hon. member used the term he used in describing the recreational organization in his own constituency as a gambling joint. By doing so I am sure, whether he intended to do it or not, he has cast aspersions upon a great many organizations in our country, including Legion clubs, church organizations and service clubs which carry on exactly the same type of activity in order to raise finances for their various organizations.
I want to make it perfectly clear that even on the basis of what the hon. member himself said, his own description of the activities of this organization in his constituency, that organization is certainly operating strictly within the law. It is a non-profit organization. There is no question of income tax involved in the operations of this organization. With regard to their raising finances in order to support the political party of their choice, I would consider it to be one of the finest ways in which to do it. Certainly it is much better for the people who wish to support the party of their choice to get together in the form of an organization and voluntarily contribute toward that cause than for a party to depend upon large contributions by interested corporations.
The hon. member tried to slough off the donations made by the breweries to his party in the province of Manitoba by saying, "Well, it is a mere $30,000". He is aware, as is everybody else, that it is not a question of $30,000. The party to which he belongs receives millions of dollars from various corporations across this country. This is only an indication in our own province, and the reason it has drawn more public attention than usual is the fact, as he well knows, that here is an industry that operates under a price system set up by the government of Manitoba. Their product is all sold to the government of Manitoba or to the liquor commission at a price, and that government sets the price; and it has set a price which has;

resulted in a profit of over $18 million to four breweries in that province since 1946.
It is perfectly improper in my view, and I think in the view of the people of Manitoba, that an industry which deals so closely and intimately with the government of that province should offer financial contributions for political purposes to the party in power. That does not exonerate the other parties that participate in those contributions, but they do not have the same responsibility. The Liberal party in that province must bear the responsibility, because it is in power, of having received contributions from breweries which operate under a price system set up by that government. I regret that the hon. member tried to wriggle out of that position by attempting to cast aspersions upon a perfectly legitimate recreational organization that operates within the law, does nothing wrong and voluntarily makes contributions toward the party of its choice.
I would be perfectly satisfied if the Liberal party in Canada were to operate on the same basis. They could have any number of clubs set up for the purpose of raising finances for their party, and I would not have one word to say in objection because I think it is a legitimate way and a good way in which to raise finances. But it is not a good way when contributions are made by huge corporations that deal intimately with the government.
Perhaps the most classic example we have had in very recent days is Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. Here is a company that has, through the medium of the government, dipped into the public treasury in order to finance its operations. If that corporation is found to be making huge financial contributions for political purposes to the party in power, the people of Canada will have a perfect right to feel suspicious and to feel that they are being sold down the river.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose one might say that the taxation division of any government is always the most unpopular branch of it, human nature being what it is. I might even go as far as to say that such has probably been the case ever since the days of Pharaoh, the Romans and King Herod. I think, therefore, that any observations a person might make on this particular item of these estimates should be of a general and a constructive nature to try to assist the minister and the officials of his department in correcting certain abuses that I think exist at the present time. The estimates of this department were before the special committee on estimates, and as a result there are certain general observations and recommendations I should like to make. I feel that these conclusions could be drawn from the evidence that was brought before that committee.
First of all, with respect to succession duties I should like to mention the question of the valuation of real estate. As hon. members know, the federal government has its own system of succession duties and certain of the provinces have their systems. As a result of having two different administrations frequently, not in all cases, Mr. Chairman, the provincial authorities and the federal authorities arrive at different valuations on the same piece of real estate. We can all understand how that comes about, because of course the federal department has no right to tell the provincial departments how to value real estate and vice versa. These niceties of distinction as between governments are not so apparent to the ordinary person on the street; and the general public can see no sense in the federal government valuing a property at $30,000 and the provincial department valuing it at $35,000. I think there is some justification for that attitude.
I know there are great difficulties in trying to arrive at uniformity in this matter, but one reasonable recommendation that might be made would be for the federal Department of National Revenue to try harder to work out some arrangements with the provinces whereby valuations could be uniform. I repeat that we all know there are difficulties, but the ordinary man on the street does not understand these things and it does not bring any government, be it federal or provincial, into better respect if we have this situation where one office values real estate at one

Supply-National Revenue amount and another office at another amount. Undoubtedly some arrangement could be worked out if a real effort were made and a common system of valuations, even common valuators, could be arranged in most parts of the country. Then one valuation for the provincial and federal succession duties could be arrived at.
The second thing with respect to succession duties is this. I feel that the department should issue new directives and instructions with respect to the procedure to be followed. I think these new directives and instructions should be complete, clear and concise. They should be uniform. They should leave no room for ambiguity, particularly with respect to certain matters which are as follows. First, disclosure to executors and legal representatives of estates should be made as soon as possible of the rules and regulations that the legal representative or executor should take into consideration before assessment of the assets is made by the department. In this respect I think it should be made clear also to the local officers that the government does not have the attitude, as the minister told us in committee, of "get all you can." This has been mentioned by other hon. members this afternoon. The minister made it quite clear to us in the committee that this was not the attitude of the government. There seems to be some misunderstanding in this respect, and if new directives were sent out it could be made quite clear that this was not the attitude of the government. Annoyance and difficulty as between the government department and the taxpayer could thus be avoided.
Another thing that should be made quite clear to the members of the department and the local offices-and again the minister pointed out very clearly in the committee that this was not the policy of his department- concerns their attitude that they are not missionaries. I have heard numerous complaints from reliable authorities that the local offices have the idea they are not missionaries and they will not disclose to executors or legal representatives of estates rules that might be helpful. As I have said, apparently the attitude of some officials in local offices is, "We are not missionaries". I think a directive from the department should make it quite clear to these local officials that this is not to be the case. The minister has told us that in the committee, and I think it should be made clear to these officials.
I believe it should be made clear to these officials as well that promotions are not the result of "getting all you can." The minister made it clear to us in committee that this was not the policy the department follows in


naming promotions. As I pointed out on other occasions I know a great many people, not only in the Department of National Revenue but in totally unrelated and non-government departments, who have the idea that they stand a better chance of promotion if they take this attitude. If the minister made it quite clear to the officials of local departments that they are much more likely to get promotion by giving all the information possible to legal representatives and executors and by doing everything they can to be helpful, further annoyance and further difficulty as between the department and the general public would be alleviated.
Those last two remarks of mine might also be applied to the income tax branch of the department. Another matter I should like to mention is this question of the valuation of what you might call the non-liquid assets of the estate. As hon. members know, when a man dies the assets in his estate are valued as of the date of death. There is no difficulty with things such as stocks, bonds, cash in the bank, mortgages and so on. Frequently the difficulty arises when you get fairly large estates, possibly between $50,000 and $150,000, where the assets are not liquid, in other words not easily disposed of. This situation occurs when you get large farms, and in the southern part of Ontario this applies to tobacco farms and fruit farms. Fortunately it does not often apply to dairy farms, but to the more specialized type of farming such as tobacco and fruit farming. It applies also to various types of businesses. You may have a small garage business or a merchandising business which may be worth $200,000 or $300,000. Even a specialized type of farm may be worth $50,000 or $150,000 under normal conditions when it can be sold without any rush.
However, as hon. members know the succession duty must be paid within a certain period of time. Very often while the valuation of the property is taken as of the date of death, when there is no ready cash available to pay the succession duties these farms or businesses have to be sold at a considerable sacrifice in order to raise the cash to pay the succession duty. As a result the estate, instead of being worth let us say $150,000, may only be worth $80,000 or $90,000; yet the taxes have to be paid on the higher figure. We all understand that there is to be a new act introduced this session, the estates act I believe it is to be called, and I hope when that act comes down this disagreeable stiuation will be remedied.
There is another item which does not come under succession duties but I will include it for convenience sake, and that is the matter of joint tenancy. I would say that a property

owned jointly by a husband and wife should not be taxable as a gift even if it amounts to over $4,000, in other words if the property is worth over $8,000, even if the wife contributed nothing, provided that all the surrounding facts show that the property was placed in a joint tenancy only for convenience in case the husband dies.
I may say that this is a very common procedure in Ontario, and I have no doubt elsewhere as well. A young couple get married and buy a house. The conveyance is in their joint names. In some provinces lawyers and conveyances will put the property in their joint names. As I say, this is a matter of convenience; it is a matter of protecting the wife. If the man dies the property will automatically go to her. Because of the present prices of houses it is not uncommon-in fact it is quite usual-for people to pay more than $8,000 for a house. If all the surrounding facts show that the property is in fact the property of the husband, that he pays all the taxes and carries out all the dealings in connection with the property, if it is in the name of the husband and wife only for convenience sake, then there should be no question of a gift tax.
The regulations require that today as a matter of policy. There is little doubt, Mr. Chairman, that policy and procedure cannot help but overlap to a certain extent. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I would go so far as to say that the family home-I repeat, only the family home-should be considered as jointly owned by husband and wife, if they so desire it, with no question of gift tax at all. I think that is a socially desirable thing. Young couples start out by buying a piece of property. After all, the wife does contribute to the value of the home. She looks after the children, cooks the meals and maintains the property. I do not think the Department of National Revenue or the government would be out very much money if the husband and wife could consider their home-and I say only their home, not any other property-jointly owned so that no gift tax would be payable at all.
I should now like to say a word with respect to income tax. I think it is rather a pity, Mr. Chairman, that the amendments to the Income Tax Act proposed by the hon. member for Kamloops were not adopted. That is past history now. We hope that in the future they may be considered more favourably by the Minister of Finance. However, I should like to recommend that directives be sent out to ensure uniformity of procedure in all local offices of the income tax division. Those directives should be clear 67509-319
Supply-National Revenue and concise. According to the evidence given recently in the committee on estimates that is not always the case.

Regardless of what the situation is, I do not think it is good policy for the departmental officials to make investigations on complaints received by letter. Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise one question of administrative efficiency having to do with the deduction of income tax at the source and the liability of the employee for such taxes. In effect you have two parties responsible for the payment of the taxes, the employer whose duty it is to deduct and remit the taxes and the employee whose duty it is to pay the taxes. Perhaps the minister could tell the committee how this administrative problem is handled. I had noted some questions I should like to ask. Is there a file for the employer with respect to each employee? Is there also a separate file with respect to each employee? Which is the control file? How is information passed from one file to the other? Does the same member of the administrative staff have the responsibility for both files?
I ask these questions because there is a problem in connection with collection and not demanding the same taxes where two people are responsible. I have a case which I intend to cite to the minister. A Miss Marjorie E. Dixon was employed as a temporary stenographer in certain law offices, moving about from one to the other. The case the hon. gentleman refers to indicates the small errors that can occur in any office or in any business. In the set of tables which are distributed before the beginning of the year are set out the deductions that should be made relative to weekly wages or annual salaries. Those deductions are to be made from the employee's salary and remitted to the district office before the 15th of the following month. The director of the district office is the person who has full charge of that, no matter which official or set of officials of the division it is referred to. At the end of the year he sends in a form which indicates the total deductions that have been made from the salary of that employee throughout the year or, if he has not been employed by the same person, the number and the amount of the deductions made. The employee himself fills in a form, his return, and he says that he has had deducted $10 per pay or per month, or a total of $120. Those two are put together in that district office, and if they do not correspond then we attempt to find out where the discrepancy has arisen.
It may well happen that there has been a change in the rate of payment. That employee may have worked for only six months, so he may have had three or four jobs in the one year. If so, then he has deduction slips from these different people. I may say that with the millions of returns-and it runs into millions-where money is deducted at

It was my intention, Mr. Chairman, to comment on some of the matters that were discussed by the hon. member for Hamilton West, but I noticed that later the Minister of Finance suggested that she had been given quite a bit of latitude and I think the implication of the minister's suggestion was that he hoped others would not claim the same latitude. I assure him that I shall not do so. I should like, however, just to say in a sentence or two that I was glad that the hon. lady raised once again the question of the floor under medical expenses.
In spite of the fact that the house has made a decision on that matter at this session, and despite the fact that no change in that regard has been included in this year's budget, I hope the Minister of Finance will give consideration to it in preparation of that next budget which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration reminded him earlier he might be making before the end of this parliament. Whether or not there will be another budget before the end of this parliament is not a certainty, but if there is one I hope he will do something about that floor. If he follows the practice of recent years he will reduce it another notch. That is better than leaving it where it is, but I hope that next time he will wipe it out altogether.
Now I turn to two or three things which I believe are administrative rather than in the policy field, though the first one may be on the borderline between administration and policy. On several occasions cases have been brought to my attention similar to one about which I received a letter a short while ago. This is the case of a taxpayer, a married man, who is contributing rather heavily to the support of a widowed sister in law who has a number of children. The taxpayer and his wife are both working now, although that gets away from the main point about which I am concerned, for the result is that the taxpayer in question has to file his return on a single basis.
However, what did disappoint him greatly when he went to the officer in charge-this was in Toronto, I may say-was to discover that there was not any way in which he could claim the deduction for the children of his widowed sister in law, who of course are his nephews and nieces. The officials whom he saw in the Toronto office read to him section 26 of the Income Tax Act. When he saw the part that refers to child or children without any reference to them belonging to the taxpayer, he was hopeful that since he was contributing to the support of these children

he would be able to claim $150 or $400 deduction tor them. I believe they are all of family allowance age in this case, so the amount he was seeking was simply the $150 each. However, the officials indicated to him that the reference to child or children is only in that part of section 26 which deals with the right of the taxpayer to claim $2,000 exemption as a person who is maintaining a self-contained domestic establishment, supporting therein a child or children under 21 years of age, and so on. It was pointed out to him, on the other hand, that later in the section, indeed in the subsections where his case has to fall, the reference is to a child or grandchild. The reason I say this might be a policy matter or might be a matter of administration is that the income tax official with whom this taxpayer dealt did use the word "interpretation". He said that as the law was now being interpreted, though nieces and nephews were not excluded in a case such as his, they were not included, and therefore the official who handled this case felt that this man could not be granted this exemption.
It has been indicated to me that it is not an unusual type of case where, as the result of the death of a brother, someone else in the family does make a substantial contribution to the maintenance of the fatherless nephews and nieces. I would hope that the minister might take a look at this and see whether it is a type of case that can be dealt with by a reinterpretation of the section, by regulations based on the section or in some other way. I appeal to him to attend to it as soon as he can if it can be done in an administrative way; but if after studying it he comes to the conclusion that the matter cannot be dealt with administratively and does call for an amendment to the act, I hope he will take the matter up with his colleague the Minister of Finance. In human terms it does seem that in a case like that, where a taxpayer is contributing substantially to the support of nephews and nieces, he should have the right to deduct the $150 or $400 allowance with respect to those nephews and nieces.
The next point I draw to the minister's attention is one I have raised on various occasions in the past, but I ask him once again to study the matter of including on the T-4 slips a place for amounts deducted for trade union dues, particularly in the case of some of the large employers who handle the payment of trade union dues under a checkoff arrangement. The employer is already doing the bookkeeping involved in the checkoff, and it does seem that it would be a matter of simplicity and a matter of fairness if the T-4 slip had on it, in addition to the other items such as income tax deducted at
Supply-National Revenue the source, pension fund contributions and so on, a place for the entry of the amount of trade union dues deducted in that way.
I know that one of the answers the minister may make is that the law with regard to the deductibility of trade union dues has certain qualifications. Not everything that is paid to a trade union as dues, though it may seem to the member of the union to be dues, is allowed as dues for the purposes of the act as it now stands. However, there are some cases where everything that is paid does meet the conditions of the law; and in those cases where it does not-in other words if this issue is also part administrative and part policy-I would hope the Minister of National Revenue would deal with it himself in so far as it is administrative and make appropriate strong representations to his colleague the Minister of Finance in so far as the matter is one of policy.

My colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South has mentioned the initiation fee as one of the items involved in joining a trade union which is not allowed for purposes of income tax deductibility. It seems to me that some less complicated way could be found than now obtains with regard to the portion of trade union dues that is allowed. Just as a suggestion I throw out to the minister that instead of the complicated set-up now existing, which requires some trade union secretaries to do quite a bit of arithmetic and establish the percentage of the dues that have been paid that is allowable -and sometimes it is a percentage that runs to at least two decimal points-some ceiling on the amount could be fixed.
I have heard the fear expressed that if there were no limitations of any kind some union members might decide to pay rather fantastic sums to their unions for benefits that might come back to them so they could get the benefit of income tax deductibility in that way. I certainly do not know of any instances where a practice of that kind has been tried but, as I say, a way to avoid that would be to survey the field as to the level of trade union dues being paid. It would work out as a certain percentage of the wages of the worker, and some reasonable percentage sufficiently above that figure could be set so that everything a trade unionist paid by way of dues might be allowed as deductible for income tax purposes provided it did not go over that reasonable percentage of his wages. It does seem to me that would be a far more practical and fairer way than the one that obtains at the present time. I am free to admit that this is in part administrative and in part

Supply-National Revenue policy; therefore I am glad that I have the attention of both the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance on this point.
I move on to another suggestion I should like to make to the minister. In the page of information that is attached to the T1 short form which was put out this year there is one paragraph which reads as follows:
Income from pension fund-If you received a lump sum payment out of a pension fund during the year, the amount must be included in your income for the year but may be subject to a reduced tax rate. For further information on this point, inquire at your district taxation office.
As the minister knows, this relates to the special treatment that can be accorded a lump sum that a taxpayer receives out of a pension fund by virtue of the terms of section 36 of the Income Tax Act. As the minister also knows, earlier in the session I inquired whether the department would not consider putting out some special forms to enable people to deal with a claim they might be in a position to make under section 36 of the act. The minister did not feel that that was necessary, but drew attention to the fact that there is this paragraph in the explanatory notes attached to the income tax form.
What I wish to point out is that there is more in section 36 than is referred to in this explanatory paragraph. If one reads section 36 carefully he discovers that it is possible to get the special treatment that is accorded payments of that kind, a treatment that involves comparing the total amount of tax you paid over the past three years with the total amount of income you had over the past three years, but what I was about to say was that in addition to it being possible to get that special treatment for lump sum payments out of a pension fund there are certain other lump sum payments than can receive the same treatment.
For example, if a person is dismissed from his employment and is given a lump sum in lieu of a period of time-weeks, months, or what have you-I am told that also is the type of lump sum that can be accorded special treatment. A person can receive money because he has been retired or laid off for other reasons than going on pension. What I am suggesting at this point is that this paragraph I read from the explanatory notes that are attached to the income tax form should tell the taxpayer more than it tells him at the present time. At the moment all it tells him about what is contained in section 36 is that he can get special treatment for a lump sum payment out of a pension fund; but since the section provides for special treatment for certain other lump sum payments as well I

think some reference to them should at least be included in the explanatory notes attached to the income tax form.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw one other matter to the attention of the minister. As he knows because of the sessional papers he has tabled this year in response to questions I have placed on the order paper, it is now common knowledge that the department has on hand a rather sizeable sum of money in refunds that have not got back to the people to whom they belong. I refer to sessional papers No. 106-C and No. 106-D, both of which were tabled on Wednesday, March 14, 1956, in response to questions I had placed on the order paper. One of them had to do with wartime compulsory savings refunds. It is quite a while now since those refunds were all to be paid back to the people to whom they belong. But apparently as of January 31, 1956, there were still refunds due to some 63,203 persons. The amount on hand for those persons was $2,923,951.48. In addition to that, it turns out as follows; if I may, I should just like to read one sentence regarding income tax refunds in general from sessional paper No. 106-D:
The total amount of income tax refunds outstanding as unpaid to individuals, as of January 31, 1956, was $2,501,393.05.
If you add those two sums together you will find they add up to something over $5,400,000 of money which is in the possession of the department and which rightfully belongs to individuals across Canada.
The minister included in the sessional papers his answers to my questions as to what steps the government has taken to get these refunds to the persons to whom they belong. He indicated that a certain amount of investigation has been carried on and that a considerable amount of advertising has been done. But it still seems to me that if the government were as anxious to get this $5 million back to those people as it would be to get in the money that the same number of people might owe to the government, it could make better headway than that.
I would appeal to the minister to give some more serious thought to ways and means of finding out where these people are and getting this money to them. In all probability these people who have wartime compulsory savings refunds coming to them are little people. The so-called big people seem to know their way around with respect to getting back refunds of this kind. I am sure that while many of these refunds will not be very large sums of money, they will belong to people to whom any sum of money would be a godsend. I would urge that some serious

thought be given to finding a way of getting this money back to the people to whom it belongs.
In that connection-and in part of what I am now going to say I shall make mention of the other side of the coin-I was also interested in the question of whether there are people who have had tax deducted at the source but who, through failure to file an income tax return at the end of the year, have not got back moneys to which they are entitled. Undoubtedly there will be people-* and this ties in with the discussion that was held just a few minutes ago between the Minister of National Revenue and the hon. member for St. Paul's-from whom deductions are made at the source during the year but with respect to whom, for one reason or another, perchance because they do not work the whole year or because they move from one job to another and the rate of pay changes, when the year is done the total amount deducted at the source can be greater than the amount which the taxpayer would really be obliged to pay.
There are many people who find it difficult to dope out income tax matters and who just do not bother to file their returns. There can be people-and I am sure there are-in that category who have overpaid their income tax during the year by means of amounts deducted at the source but who, because they do not file returns, do not get their money back. This was a question I put on the order paper. It is found at page 2587 of Hansard of March 23, 1956:
1.	For each of the last five taxation years for which the statistics are available, how many persons from whom income tax was deducted at the source did not file an annual income tax return?
The reason I asked that question was as I have already indicated. I am concerned about these people who have too much deducted at the source and who do not get it back. The answer to that question was: "No information available". My next question read as follows:
2.	By years, how many of such persons were found, or believed, to have a refund coming to them?
The answer again was, "No information available". That answer rather startled me for two reasons. First of all, it seemed rather strange that there could be people making payments through deductions at the source, and overpaying during the course of the year, with the government through this department having no information about those people. In other words, by virtue of not having that information, by virtue of not checking such files, these people inadvertently are left in the position of having paid more than
Supply-National Revenue they should have paid during the year, yet they do not get their surplus back.
But what I realized when I saw that answer -though I admit that this was not what I was out for when I put the question on the order paper-is that the reverse can be true if the answers here are correct. As I interpret these answers, they seem to be at variance with what the minister was saying to the hon. member for St. Paul's in another connection a moment ago.
