It was my privilege to be a member of the estimates committee, and I just want to draw some conclusions from my experience on that committee for the benefit of the house. First of all we considered the estimates of the excise and customs branch. I was certainly very favourably impressed with the results of the work of that committee. All the questions and criticisms that were brought forward were very ably handled, and I think to the satisfaction of the committee. Very good explanations were given for the decisions and rulings that were made in cases dealing with customs and excise.
I was a bit, what shall I say, shocked at the change of pace and attitude with respect to the income tax division in that committee. It seemed apparent to some of the members -I will not say most of the members.-that there was not likely to be any admission by the department that any errors could possibly arise. In practically every case where a member brought forward a complaint there was evidence brought forward to show that somewhere along the line there was some 

mistake, and it just could not possibly be that way. There were a number of things I wanted to bring to the minister's attention in that committee, but I felt it would be futile and the result would be more or less an okay of the work of the department and discrediting, as far as possible, the member who brought forward the objections. Perhaps I am wrong, but I regret that is the feeling I brought out of that committee.
The hon. member for Kamloops introduced his bill, and I mentioned that it did not go far enough. His suggestion was that the returns should be finalized in a three-year period. I mentioned last session, and I mention it again now, that in cases involving $10,000 or less the department should be able to process the taxpayers' returns and give a final receipt-except in cases of deliberate fraud-within 12 months from April 30. The taxpayer is given 4 months after the end of the calendar year to make up his return, and surely if the department had one year from that time it would be adequate, if they are as efficient as they would like the public to believe. At that time I brought to the minister's attention the fact that many county councils signified their belief that that could be done and should be done.
The hon. member for Perth dealt very fully with the net worth statements. Therefore I shall not comment further except to say that I heartily endorse what the hon. member for Perth said yesterday. The hon. member for Hamilton West dealt with payments to retirement plans. I just want to point out here that self-employed persons are not allowed to deduct payments they may make to any retirement plan, yet self-employed persons are contributors to all these other plans because of the fact that payments become part of the costs of the things these particular companies make and sell. Consequently these self-employed persons are not allowed to deduct pension payments made on their own account but they are helping, in a way, to pay into these other retirement plans.
From time to time I have mentioned in this house the advantages of profit-sharing plans in industry and the good relations that can be developed through such plans.
These profit-sharing industries in Canada and the United States have made representations to the effect that until the profits that accrue to any employee are actually in the hands of that employee they should not be taxed; otherwise he may be taxed on funds he never will receive. Even the chambers of commerce recommended that the right to assess be limited to one year dating from the assessment, but that is not good enough because the assessment may be delayed one,

two, three, four, even five years or more, and consequently the taxpayer would not stand to gain under such a plan.
Just recently I listened to the minister, and I am going to quote what he said as recorded on page 820 of Hansard for February 2 of this year. That he of all men in the house should use these words and then have his department act as they do is something I can hardly understand. This is what he had to say:
As everyone knows from common knowledge, from time immemorial the Englishman's home has been his castle, and all matters pertaining to him and his family are protected by law from trespass or exposure. You cannot enter his house without his permission. You cannot ascertain his private affairs without voluntary disclosure. This right of privacy that every Englishman possesses is as strong in this country and in all the countries of the commonwealth as it is and has been from time immemorial in England, from whence we draw so many of our laws and so much of our tradition. This right of privacy that every Englishman possesses is, as I said, as strong in this country as in any other.
Then his department goes about denying all these things. Probably, after the furore of last week, I should not say a great deal about abuse of power, but all through history we find individuals seeking power. The more power they get the more power they want, and the more power they get the more glory they get. I would point out to the minister that power is fleeting. I need only mention a few names; Peron, Mussolini, Hitler, and all down the line. Power is fleeting, so be careful how you use that power.
The people with whom you are dealing are, in most instances, hard-working people. They are not acquainted with all the fine points of the law. In fact I intended to have on my desk the office consolidation of the Income Tax Act and all the amendments that have been added to it. The minister has heard, and I have heard, of Philadelphia lawyers, but all the lawyers in Philadelphia could not interpret them alike. Yet the taxpayer is expected to know just where he stands in connection with these many laws. Just while I am dealing with that may I say I have on my desk a letter from a constituent of mine dealing with the joint ownership of property. He says:
Six months after death of the wife income tax assessed for a few hundred dollars.
He said they had owned the property jointly for six years. He also said that a well-known firm of lawyers had advised him that no gift tax would be assessed in this particular case. Yet six months after the death of his wife he was confronted with a demand for an amount which he paid, and then of course he protested about it to me, but there he was. He goes on to say:
Supply-National Revenue When I confronted my lawyer with the statement he made to me, he said, "It is quite evident nobody knows just what the income tax department may do; nor can any ordinary citizen interpret their rules and regulations".
That is what the taxpayers are up against. They find that a rule that may be applied in one case does not apply in another. I am not blaming the minister too much. These things go on because the people in the different districts have a considerable amount of power, and perhaps these things go on without his knowledge. These usages and customs have grown up like Topsy over a period of years. I imagine the minister may admit that some of these questionable practices have gone on, but he will defend the system.
I want to point out that, on the other hand, knowing about the practices and allowing them to go on is a disgrace. If he does not know that they are going on, it is certainly time he did. We have heard a lot in years gone by about the four freedoms, the freedom from want, the freedom of religion, the freedom of speech and the freedom from fear. I mentioned this question of fear before. Not only the taxpayers, but accountants and lawyers do not want to take any part in it because they are afraid of what might happen.

When ministers refuse to share the blame for waste, inefficiency and worse in their departments, they are admitting that the job of government has grown too big for them; they are claiming, in effect, that while they should still be trusted with the direction of the nation's business, they should not be expected to worry about the people they have hired for the day to day handling of that business. I have argued it with the Department of National Defence and Department of Veterans Affairs, and it is always thrown back to national revenue. It is a rather pathetic thing. Today the services are a career for many people, and will be for a long time. The soldier, airman or sailor may contribute to a pension fund for 10 or 12 years. I have heard of cases where it was 10 years. If he dies from natural causes while in the service the pension commission says no pension is indicated because it is not attributable to service. The war veterans allowance officials say the widow cannot get anything because she is too young but that the superannuation contribution is returned to her; and the Department of National Revenue then considers that as income. In the one case I had, where the serviceman was in the forces for 10 years, the contributions were returned to the widow,


who had three small children, and the income tax division took $600 out of that refund of contributions as income tax.
I believe the Department of National Revenue should consult with the other departments concerned. They tell me they are quite willing to consider the matter provided the Department of National Revenue will also consider it, and I think this is something that should be corrected. It is bad enough for the young woman to lose her husband and be left with a small family, no income and no pension rights because her husband died from natural causes despite the fact that he was in the services, but to have the pension contributions made over a period of ten years all assessed as income in one year when they are returned is most unfair.

It is not all tax free, just the percentage that is allowed for income tax purposes, and I think in a case of that kind there are extenuating circumstances.

I think the wear and tear and the strain of war were contributing factors to the man's death.

Over the years the municipalities have advanced money for the installation of such drains and the loans have been repaid over a normal period of 20 years. Some 40 years ago, when money was more expensive than it is now, it used to take $8 for each $100 to repay the loan over a 20-year period. The rate is not as high at this time.
People who kept account of the expenses of their farming operations had always put in their taxes in one sum, and in the tax notices the tile drain loans were included. I find now that with respect to summary assessments in my area the assessors are delving into the amount represented by the carrying charges of the loan. It does not amount to a great deal for any one farm. If you reassess one farmer who has his land tiled, then it is right that every farmer who has his farm tiled should be reassessed. I contend that the amount of detail that would be involved in reassessing all the returns would not warrant the expense and would not be warranted by the amount of money that would be returned to the department.

However, I was glad to hear the hon. member for Kent a few moments ago state that the minister had said this afternoon that the net worth statement was the last resort of the department in dealing with these matters. Frankly, I find it rather difficult to understand that statement, Mr. Chairman. Although I have not been very close to these matters during the last few years owing to the fact that we are here from January until July or August, at least in previous years one of my jobs was to deal with scores of these matters every year in my own office, and I know they are still going through the office with which I have some connection.
I may say that I do not think these net worth statements are entirely the last resort. You get farmers who file their income tax returns, and assume that everything is all right. Then suddenly, for no apparent reason, the inspectors appear, start investigating the affairs of the farmer and then a net worth statement is submitted to him. The farmer is faced with this situation.
I must say this. I think the inspectors who handle these matters are perhaps dealing more courteously with the taxpayers today than they did in the past. They are not as brusque. They are not quite as-shall we say, to use a polite term-dynamic as they were a few years ago. I think the complaints which have been raised in this committee during these years with respect to these net worth statements have had a considerable influence on the department. I want to compliment the minister for the progress which has been made.
After all, what is the situation with respect to these net worth statements? Yesterday


afternoon we had a speech by the hon. member for Perth who spent considerable time in this committee dealing with the net worth statements and complaining of the way in which they are sometimes administered. Last night we had the hon. member for Dauphin also reiterating those statements and emphasizing their importance. Then we had the speech by the hon. member for Kent. Although he did not commit himself in any way, I think it is a fair inference, when he expressed his pleasure that the net worth statement was the last resort, that he is not too happy about the way in which they have been administered. Then you have myself at the moment speaking for Nova Scotia on the same matter.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre said the other day in another debate, when you have reasonable men who are aroused or, as in this case, concerned about a matter, I think it is something which should impress itself upon the minister. You have these members from various parts of Canada who are still saying that the way in which these net worth statements are administered is something to which, to put it mildly, the minister should give very careful consideration.
What is the situation? A farmer is confronted with a net worth statement. He is told, "If you can prove we are wrong, we will accept it. You prove that we are wrong". How can that be done by a farmer whose records are usually somewhat incomplete-at least I am speaking for the farmers whom I know, namely those in Nova Scotia-and who does not purport to keep records over a long period of years? He is confronted with a net worth statement and is told that by the inspector, as I say, very politely and very courteously. It is somewhat different from what they used to say.
I emphasize that point again. There has been a change in the way in which they deal with these matters. Nevertheless, they say, "If you can prove we are wrong, we will be very glad to hear from you; otherwise this statement stands". What is the farmer going to do? As we all know, under the act the inspector goes back for six years without any question; and if there is an allegation of fraud-we will use that term-then he can go back to the inception of the act and we are back to 1917.
The farmer just cannot present details, invoices or anything of that kind which can meet that situation. I can speak with some feeling on this matter because, as I said, at least in earlier years I had to deal with scores and scores of these cases every year, and I felt that in many cases men whom I knew to be honest, men whom I knew were

trying to file a proper return, who thought they had filed it and who had paid the tax which they believed was due, were subsequently confronted with these net worth statements and were embarrassed and sometimes seriously penalized because of that procedure.
Again I repeat that I want to give the department full credit for the fact that there has been an improvement in this approach. I am only stressing the matter now in order to urge on the minister that he consider again this whole matter and try to improve still more the approach to it.
I read the evidence given in the committee, of which I was not a member. I heard the statement of the minister and the officials to the effect that there was no scrutiny of the taxpayer's affairs and that these net worth statements were made only because of investigation which had been made and when they found something irregular. Perhaps the farmer bought a brand new Buick when he reported a loss the year before, and therefore the department thought the matter worthy of scrutiny.
I can tell the minister that I have heard inspectors of his department say, "We were driving down the road; we saw where you were building a new fireplace on the outside of your house, so we came in to investigate and see what was going on". Another time I was told that they said, "Your wife was seen in Kentville and we saw her with a new fur coat. We did not know how you could buy a fur coat for your wife". Whether it was a Christmas present from her father did not make any difference. They said, "We did not think you could buy a fur coat for your wife. We therefore decided to have you investigated and we are now presenting this net worth statement".
As the hon. member for Perth emphasized last night, I realize and quite admit that there are times when net worth statements are necessary. I know that all farmers, 100 per cent of them, have no monopoly on virtue. There may be the odd one-I do not think there are many-who perhaps has been a little bit light on his pencil when he has filled in his income and a little bit heavy when he marked down his expenditures. That has been known to happen. I am willing to admit that it even happens with farmers, although I doubt if it happens very often. There may be the occasional justification for a net worth statement and a farmer being assessed on that basis.
I want to say to the minister with all the seriousness I can command that I do think, whatever may have been the improvement in the technique of his officials, the improvement in the approach to this thing,
Supply-National Revenue there is one phase of that net worth statement in which they have refused to face the facts of life, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Perth last night. That is when these inspectors continually and universally insist upon a cost of living being assessed against the farmer which is out of proportion with the realities of the situation.
I suppose in earlier days I have gone over scores and scores of these statements every year. In almost every case I know the farmer was assessed on a cost of living basis which was greatly in excess of that which he actually paid. You get his assets and you will find he has paid a little bit off the mortgage, a little bit off the bank loan or bought a new tractor. Then you say it costs him $2,400 or $200 per month to live. It did not cost him that. Very often it did not cost him half that. Very often he is assessed on that basis and the officials very generously say, "If you can prove we are wrong we will accept it".
From my own personal experience I have seen scores and scores of men whom I know have been treated unjustly on that net worth statement basis, and particularly the cost of living item. I hope that is something the minister will consider very, very carefully. I cannot join with the hon. member for Cape Breton South, who said a while ago he hoped the minister would be back here next year. Personally I hope he will not be back, and unless he reconsiders this matter of the net worth statement his chances of coming back are very dim indeed.
There is another matter to which I wish to direct his attention in connection with the rural economy, and that is the right to elect. I know that now possibly we are verging on the statute or on policy rather than on administration, but I think the dividing line in this case is so narrow the minister will not raise a point of order. As the hon. member for Moose Jaw pointed out last night, I think there has been legislation by administration in this department anyway in dealing with capital gains. All those who are interested in the rural economy have seen farmers who were selling property, some of whom have been assessed on a capital gains basis without any change whatever in this legislation, and they realize that the dividing line between administration and legislation is very narrow indeed. I am not going to develop that now because I am speaking mainly from an agricultural standpoint.
It always has nettled me that farmers who happen to employ an auditor like the hon. member for Perth or perhaps retain a lawyer
505$

Supply-National Revenue like the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and get advice, can just file a statement about electing and thereafter can average. If they do not file that statement then they cannot average. I realize that the right to average applies to others than farmers. It applies to businessmen and to people in other walks of life. They always have their auditors or solicitors to give them continual advice.
However, I think the thing is perhaps somewhat outmoded today. I believe most of them today know about the right of election, but I can say from my own small experience in a very limited area that I have seen hundreds of farmers treated unjustly because they were not advised of the fact that to average they had to elect before the first day of May or whatever it was. Not having done that and having had one good year and four bad years, two before and two after, but not having averaged, they were ruined. I have always thought it could have been part of the act that they should have been given the right to elect and to average. The question may be somewhat academic today because I think the practice is fairly widespread, but certainly it is purely a matter of administration.
I had a case before the officials here within the last six months in which a farmer had not averaged so that a gross injustice was being done to him as compared to his neighbour across the street, who had averaged. I say that from the standpoint of administration, you should consider these cases and perhaps legislate by administration by saying. "We can assume that you averaged". However, the officials always say, "Well, it is too bad you did not put that in; it is not date stamped on the first day of May. Therefore your election is out." That is something which, as I say, has nettled me because I have felt it was an absolute injustice.
Then the third thing and the only other matter I shall bring to the attention of the minister tonight, again from a rural standpoint, is the matter of the gift tax in so far as it affects farmers' sons in this country. Again I am speaking of my own area, the only area of which I have intimate knowledge. In Nova Scotia a farmer may have one son or perhaps if the farm is large enough two sons who remain with him on the understanding that when the farmer retires or dies they are going to take over the farm. The farmers there being economical and sometimes afraid of legal fees-I do not know why they should be afraid of lawyers in Nova Scotia, but some of them are perhaps a little bit afraid of lawyers

or the probate fees because they think they, are astronomical when we all know they are not-perhaps five years before they die deed the farm over to the son or to the two sons.
I can recall several years ago when the Minister of National Revenue and this government took great credit for the fact that they were raising the ceiling on succession duties. Thereafter you would only have to pay succession duties on X dollars instead of as heretofore on Y dollars. That sounded wonderful. What happened? In my constituency within three months after that change had been made there were at least 10 different farmers sons in my office- when I say "sons" they were not youths but some of them were 35 or 40 years of age- whose fathers had died and they had taken over the farms. The Department of National Revenue came along and said they owed a gift tax, sometimes of $2,000 or $2,500 or $3,000. This was the gift tax on this farm which had been deeded by the father to the son.
Now, with an expert or fairly competent legal advice, it is an easy matter to meet that situation. You can always bring forth an agreement of some kind, and I do not think the department insists that it be in writing. There can be an agreement whereby the son stays on the farm, and so forth. Some farmers who could employ a lawyer and spend quite a lot of money could perhaps beat that.
But I know scores of farmers' sons who have had to pay substantial gift taxes simply because the farmer deeded the farm over to them before he died instead of willing it to them. Certainly that was not the intent of this act and that certainly is more than a matter of administration. I know the provisions of the gift tax act provide for a gift of $4,000 to one person, per annum $1,000 to each child or 50 per cent of the difference between your income tax and your taxable income. Those matters can be applied in gifts of securities and various other things. But when you are dealing with a father who has deeded his farm to his son, who has lived on that farm from the time he was born until he was perhaps 35 or 40 when his father died and he took it over, you find that the department comes back and says, "Two years before your father died, unfortunately, instead of deeding this farm and taking back a mortgage he gave it to you." The father could have written off $4,000 per year; there are other things that could be pulled off-perhaps that is a slang expression-a dozen other legal expedients

which all of us know and which the department would welcome, but instead of getting legal advice they fall into that trap and are penalized. I know of one man who, before he got legal advice, had been assessed and borrowed $3,500 from the bank to pay the government tax, which he certainly did not owe morally, and thereafter was broke.
That is a matter of administration. As I see it, I think the department should scrutinize these transactions much more carefully in the future than it has in the past, and when it comes to that particular type of transaction, a transfer between father and son of a farm, I say the administration as such should not even suggest that a gift tax be paid.
These are all the matters I want to bring up at the moment. There are a whole host of matters that I could deal with. I am speaking from the standpoint of a member for a rural constituency and of problems with which I have been associated personally during all the years I have been in practice.

This city is the heart of the agricultural area of Manitoba. I know from personal experience that people communicate with me constantly for information concerning income tax problems. In every case we have to make a pilgrimage to Winnipeg to obtain that information. We do not mind going to Winnipeg, but we would much rather stay in Brandon if it were possible.
During the month just preceding the final date for filing income tax returns there are two officials who come out and establish themselves in the lobby of the post office. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can well understand the hon. gentleman's desire to have a public office in his community. It adds a little to his prestige, but do not forget these things cost quite a bit of money. It costs about three times as much to collect $100 in a small office like Brandon as it would in a larger office. Our average rate for collecting money is about 87 cents per hundred dollars. We know, from the experience we had with one small office in the west at Prince Albert, that it costs between $3 and $4 to collect $100 in these small offices. We have to take into consideration the costs. We believe we can do the work more efficiently in the city of Winnipeg than we could if we had three or four offices.
We have difficulty in getting assessors of the right type. In order to man an office in
Supply-Labour
Brandon we would have to have corporation assessors, individual income tax assessors and a full staff even in that smaller office. It is for that reason we have concentrated our offices in the larger cities and in places where we believe the best service can be given. It is a long way from Vancouver, with difficult transportation facilities and all the rest of it. But I will give you a very frank answer. I think Brandon can be equally well served by Winnipeg and at much less cost than if we had an office in your city. I can conclude by saying we are not putting an office in Brandon at this particular time.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENT ON TELEVISION PROGRAM
speechtext: With regard to the question of cost, it might mean a slight additional expense to the department; but I should like to point out to the minister that it also represents a considerable cost to the farmers who have to go all the way to Winnipeg to settle any income tax problems they might have.
